intents.title: Getting started
examples: how should we start
where do I begin
what should I do first
I am new, how do I use this app
how do I get started with my exercises
intents.answer: Here is how to start: 1) Make sure your health profile is complete (Profile tab), so your safety limits are set. 2) Open AI-assisted treatment planning and tap Retrieve physical treatment to get plans that suit you, then select one. 3) Open My treatment plan from the Treatment tab and start the first exercise: read its steps, then record yourself doing it. 4) The app checks your posture; reach 80% to move on to the next exercise. Your reminders follow the plan's weekly schedule.

intents.title: How to do the exercises
examples: how do I do the exercises
what is the correct way to do this exercise
how do I know my form is right
can you explain the steps
am I doing the exercise properly
intents.answer: Each exercise in your plan has its own steps and safety points: open it from your treatment pathway. Move slowly and smoothly, keep breathing, and stay within a comfortable range. Record yourself doing it and the app will check your posture and tell you what to correct. You can also ask me how to do a specific exercise, for example "how do I do the heel raise?"

intents.title: Pain or discomfort
examples: my knee hurts when I exercise
is it normal to feel sore after exercising
what should I do if I feel pain
my muscles ache the next day
my joints feel stiff
intents.answer: Some muscle tiredness or mild soreness for a day or two is normal when you start, and it should ease as you get used to the exercises. Pain that is sharp, gets worse while you exercise, or comes with swelling is not normal. Which describes your pain best? Choose an option below.

intents.title: How often and how long
examples: how often should I exercise
can I do this every day
how many times a week
how long should each session be
should I take rest days
what time of day is best
intents.answer: Follow the number of sessions per week shown in your plan, with a rest day in between when you can. Each session only takes a few minutes, and any time of day that suits you is fine, as long as it is not straight after a big meal. Your reminders already follow this schedule. Doing the exercises well matters more than doing extra sessions.

intents.title: Missed a session
examples: I missed my session yesterday
what if I skip a day
I forgot to exercise
how do I catch up
intents.answer: That is fine. Do your next session as usual; do not do two sessions in one day to catch up. If you have missed several days, start again gently with fewer repetitions and build back up.

intents.title: Exercising safely
examples: is it safe for me to exercise
how do I avoid falling
should I hold my breath
do I need to warm up
what precautions should I take
intents.answer: Exercise next to a sturdy chair or counter, on a dry non-slip floor, and breathe normally; never hold your breath. Warm up with a few minutes of gentle movement first. Stop if you feel dizzy, short of breath, or unwell. Your plan already stays within the safety limits from your health profile.

intents.title: Exercising with a health condition
examples: I have diabetes, is there anything special I should do
can I exercise with high blood pressure
I have asthma, any advice
intents.answer: Your plan was chosen within the safety limits for the conditions in your health profile, so you can follow it as set. Stop and rest if anything feels wrong, and check with your doctor before doing more than the plan.

intents.title: What you need
examples: what equipment do I need
do I need weights
what kind of chair should I use
what should I wear
do I need to buy anything
can I do it on the bed
intents.answer: You do not need to buy anything. Most exercises use a firm chair without wheels or armrests, pushed against a wall; a sofa or bed is too soft. Floor exercises need a mat or a carpet, and step-ups need a low step (no higher than 15 cm) with a rail. Wear comfortable clothes and non-slip shoes. A small water bottle can be used as a light weight if you are comfortable.

intents.title: Too easy or too hard
examples: the exercises are too easy
this is too hard for me
I can't finish all the repetitions
can I make it harder
can I do more repetitions
intents.answer: If an exercise is too hard, do fewer repetitions with good form and rest between them; it should feel like effort, not pain. If it feels too easy, keep the same plan until you finish it, then request a new recommendation from the planning page: it will suggest a plan for your new level. Do not add weight, extra sets or other exercises on your own.

intents.title: Feeling tired or unwell
examples: I feel too tired to exercise
I am exhausted after the session
I'm not feeling well today
should I exercise when I am sick
intents.answer: Feeling a little tired after exercising is normal. If you are unusually exhausted, unwell, or have a fever, skip today's session and rest; continue when you feel better. If tiredness lasts for days or comes with breathlessness, contact your doctor.

intents.title: Weak or unsteady legs
examples: my leg feels wobbly when standing
my legs feel weak
I feel unsteady on my feet
my knee gives way
I lose my balance
intents.answer: Legs that feel weak or wobbly are common after a long period of less activity, and this is what your exercises are building up. Always keep one hand on a sturdy chair or counter, do fewer repetitions, and rest when the shaking starts. If weakness comes on suddenly, or affects one side of your body, stop and get medical help straight away.

intents.title: Recording your exercise video
examples: how do I record my exercise
where should I put my phone
the app cannot detect my body
why does it say my full body is not visible
how long should the video be
intents.answer: Put your phone on a stand, upright, at about waist height and 2.5 to 3 metres away, so your whole body from head to feet stays in the picture during the movement. Use good light in front of you and record 10 to 30 seconds. Each exercise says whether the camera should face you or be at your side. Someone else may hold the phone for you if it stays still. If the app cannot see your whole body, step back a little and record again.

intents.title: Understanding your posture score
examples: what does my posture score mean
why is my accuracy low
what do I do if I fail the posture check
should I retry the exercise
intents.answer: The posture score shows how closely your movement matched the correct form, as a percentage, with tips on what to change. At 80% or more your progress is updated automatically. Below that you can read the tips and retry, or continue; every attempt is saved so you can see your improvement. If it counted fewer repetitions than you did, make each one a full, clear movement with a short pause back at the start, and keep your whole body in the picture.

intents.title: When to exercise
examples: when is the best time to exercise
can I exercise now
is it ok to exercise at night
should I exercise in the morning or evening
intents.answer: The best time is when you feel alert and have had a light meal about an hour before. Many people find late morning or late afternoon easiest. Keep to a regular time so it becomes a habit, and avoid the last hour or two before bed.

intents.title: How the app works
keywords: how do i use this app
examples: how does this app work
how do I use this app
intents.answer: HealthGuide has five tabs. Home shows today's session and your daily limits. Treatment holds your plan: get one in AI-assisted treatment planning, then do each exercise and record it so the app can check your posture. Profile holds your health details, which keep your advice safe. You can ask me about any of these at any time. You need an internet connection to sign in, check your posture and chat with me; your reminders still arrive without one.

intents.title: Your doctor's advice
examples: my doctor said I should rest for a week
the physiotherapist told me not to do squats
intents.answer: Always follow your doctor's or physiotherapist's advice first: it is based on examining you. If they told you to rest, pause your exercises (you can switch reminders off) and continue when they say it is safe; your progress is kept. If their advice differs from your plan, ask them which exercises are suitable, and update your health profile if anything has changed.

intents.title: Clicking or cracking joints
examples: my shoulder clicks when I raise my arm
my knee makes a cracking sound
is the clicking normal
intents.answer: Clicking or cracking without pain is common and usually harmless; it is often gas or a tendon moving over the joint. Carry on if it does not hurt. If it comes with pain, swelling, or the joint catching or locking, stop that movement and ask your doctor or physiotherapist.

intents.title: My treatment plan
examples: open my exercises
where are my exercises
take me to my treatment plan
intents.answer: Your treatment plan shows your exercises in order. Open the next one, read its steps, then record yourself doing it; the app checks your posture and moves you on when you reach 80%.

intents.title: Your health profile
examples: how do I update my health profile
why is my risk level high
how do I change my weight
where can I add my health conditions
intents.answer: Your health profile holds your age, gender, weight, height, health conditions and physical limitations. Your risk level and safety limits are worked out from it, and your treatment plans are chosen to fit them. Tap the button below, then Edit, to change anything; keep it up to date so your advice stays safe.

intents.title: Exercise reminders
examples: how do I change my reminder time
I am not getting reminders
how do I turn off reminders
intents.answer: Your reminders follow your plan's weekly schedule. Open Reminders to change the time or switch a reminder off and on. If none arrive, check that notifications are allowed for HealthGuide in your phone settings. If you have already exercised that day, the reminder is skipped. The reminder sound and volume follow your phone's notification settings.

intents.title: Your past results
examples: where can I see my past results
how did I do in my last session
show my session history
intents.answer: Every exercise you record is saved with its posture score and tips. Session history shows them all, with your average, your best score and a chart of how your posture accuracy is changing.

intents.title: Changing your plan or reminders
examples: how do I change my plan
can I get a different plan
how do I stop this plan
intents.answer: To change plan, open AI-assisted planning and choose Retrieve physical treatment to get new recommendations; selecting a new plan replaces the current one. You can stop a plan from the Physical Treatment page. Reminders follow your plan's weekly schedule; check that notifications are allowed for the app in your phone settings if they do not appear.

intents.title: Forgot password
examples: I forgot my password
how do I reset my password
I can't log in
how do I change my password
intents.answer: You can set a new password with a 6-digit code sent to your email: tap the button below (or Forgot password? on the login screen), enter your email, then type the code and your new password. If the code does not arrive, check your spam folder and wait a minute before asking for a new one. After too many wrong passwords the account is locked for 15 minutes.

intents.title: Verification code
examples: I did not get the verification code
the code is not working
how do I verify my email
intents.answer: The 6-digit code is sent to the email you registered with. Check your spam or junk folder, and make sure the address is spelled correctly. You can tap Resend code once a minute; a code stops working after a while, so always use the newest one. If you clicked a link in the email instead, return to the app and log in.

intents.title: Account and login
examples: how do I log in
how do I update my health profile
is my data private
intents.answer: Log in with the email and password you registered with, or use Continue with Google. If you forgot your password, tap Forgot password? on the login screen to get a reset code by email. You can update your health details on the Profile page; your plan's safety limits are recalculated when you save. Your data is only visible to your own account.

intents.title: Mild soreness or tiredness
examples: it is only mild soreness
my muscles are a bit sore the next day
intents.answer: Mild soreness is a normal sign that your muscles are working. Keep exercising gently, move within a comfortable range, and it should ease within a day or two. If it lasts longer than three days, do fewer repetitions and contact your physiotherapist.

intents.title: Sharp or worsening pain
examples: I get a sharp pain during the exercise
the pain is getting worse
intents.answer: Stop the exercise that causes it and rest. Do not push through sharp or worsening pain. If it does not settle within a day, or it stops you moving normally, contact your doctor or physiotherapist before you continue with that exercise.

intents.title: Swelling, redness or heat
examples: my knee is swelling after exercise
the joint looks red and feels warm
intents.answer: Stop exercising that joint and rest it, raised if you can. Swelling, redness or heat in a joint should be checked: contact your doctor or physiotherapist before exercising it again. If the swelling is severe or you also have a fever, seek medical care today.

intents.title: Medicines
examples: can I take painkillers before exercising
should I stop my medicine
what medicine should I take
intents.answer: I cannot give advice about medicines. Please ask your doctor or pharmacist, and keep taking your medicines as prescribed unless they tell you otherwise.

intents.title: Diagnosis and seeing a doctor
examples: what is wrong with my knee
is my bone broken
do I have arthritis
do I need surgery
should I see a doctor
intents.answer: I cannot diagnose conditions or injuries. If you are worried, or a problem is not improving, please see your doctor or physiotherapist about it. If you think something is broken or seriously injured, stop exercising it and get medical care.

intents.title: Food and drink
examples: what should I eat before exercising
should I drink water
can I exercise after a meal
intents.answer: Drink some water before and after your exercises, and wait about an hour after a large meal before exercising. For food advice that suits your health conditions, use the Diet section of the app.

intents.title: Greeting
examples: hello
hi there
good morning
intents.answer: Hello! I can answer questions about your rehabilitation exercises, pain, safety, your plan, recording your videos and reminders. Tap a topic below or type your question.

intents.title: Thanks
examples: thank you
thanks a lot
that was helpful
intents.answer: You're welcome. Keep it up! Ask me anything else about your plan, or tap Exit Chatbot when you are done.

intents.title: Okay
examples: ok
alright
got it
intents.answer: Okay. If you have another question about your exercises, pain, safety or your plan, type it or tap a topic below.

intents.title: Goodbye
examples: bye
that's all for now
intents.answer: Take care, and see you at your next session. Tap Exit Chatbot to return to the planning page.

intents.title: About this assistant
examples: what can you do
what can I ask you
are you a real person
intents.answer: I am the rehabilitation assistant for your treatment plan. I answer common questions using answers prepared in advance, so I cannot diagnose or give medical advice. You can ask about how to do your exercises, pain, safety, how often to exercise, recording your video, your posture score, and your plan or reminders.

sit_to_stand.name: Sit-to-Stand
sit_to_stand.instruction: Sit on a firm chair with feet flat and hip-width apart. Lean slightly forward and stand up fully without using your hands, then sit back down slowly. Safety: keep a stable chair against a wall; stop if you feel dizzy or knee pain.
sit_to_stand.camera: side view, whole body in frame

shoulder_abduction.name: Shoulder Abduction
aliases: raise my arms to the side
shoulder_abduction.instruction: Stand tall with arms by your sides. Raise both arms out to the side up to shoulder height with elbows straight, hold for one second, and lower slowly. Safety: do not raise above a pain-free range.
shoulder_abduction.camera: facing you, whole body in frame

shoulder_flexion.name: Shoulder Flexion
shoulder_flexion.instruction: Stand with arms by your sides. Raise both arms forward and up to shoulder height with elbows straight and thumbs up, hold for one second, and lower slowly. Safety: do not arch the back.
shoulder_flexion.camera: side view, whole body in frame

hip_abduction.name: Standing Hip Abduction
aliases: lift my leg to the side
hip_abduction.instruction: Stand beside a chair and hold it for support. Lift one leg out to the side keeping the toes forward and the body upright, then lower it. Repeat on the other side. Safety: do not lean the trunk.
hip_abduction.camera: facing you, whole body in frame

knee_extension.name: Seated Knee Extension
knee_extension.instruction: Sit upright on a chair. Straighten one knee until the leg is level with the hip, hold for two seconds, and lower slowly. Alternate legs. Safety: keep the back against the chair.
knee_extension.camera: side view, whole body in frame

elbow_flexion.name: Elbow Flexion
elbow_flexion.instruction: Stand or sit with arms by your sides, palms forward. Bend the elbows to bring the hands toward the shoulders, keeping the upper arms still against your body, then lower slowly. Use a light bottle of water if comfortable.
elbow_flexion.camera: side view, whole body in frame

wall_push_up.name: Wall Push-Up
wall_push_up.instruction: Stand an arm's length from a wall with palms on the wall at shoulder height. Bend the elbows to bring the chest toward the wall, then push back. Safety: keep the body straight from head to heels.
wall_push_up.camera: side view, whole body in frame, wall at one edge of the picture

heel_raise.name: Heel Raise
heel_raise.instruction: Stand behind a chair holding the back of it. Rise onto your toes, hold for one second, and lower slowly. Safety: keep holding the chair throughout.
heel_raise.camera: side view, whole body in frame

mini_squat.name: Mini Squat
mini_squat.instruction: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart holding a support. Bend the knees about 30 degrees keeping the heels down and the chest up, then stand up. Safety: knees must not pass the toes.
mini_squat.camera: side view, whole body in frame

seated_marching.name: Seated Marching
seated_marching.instruction: Sit upright on a chair without leaning back. Lift one knee toward the chest, lower it, and alternate legs at a steady pace.
seated_marching.camera: side view, whole body in frame

glute_bridge.name: Glute Bridge
glute_bridge.instruction: Lie on your back on a mat with knees bent and feet flat. Squeeze the buttocks and lift the hips until shoulders, hips and knees are in a straight line, then lower slowly. Safety: do not arch the lower back.
glute_bridge.camera: side view, phone on the floor about 2 m away, whole body in frame

tandem_stance.name: Tandem Stance
aliases: one foot in front of the other
tandem_stance.instruction: Stand next to a counter. Place one foot directly in front of the other, heel touching toe, and hold for 30 seconds. Switch feet. Safety: always keep one hand near the support.
tandem_stance.camera: facing you, whole body in frame

bird_dog.name: Bird Dog
bird_dog.instruction: Kneel on a mat on hands and knees, hands under shoulders, knees under hips. Stretch one arm forward and the opposite leg back until both are level with your back, hold for two seconds, return, and switch sides. Safety: keep the back flat, do not twist.
bird_dog.camera: side view, phone on the floor about 2 m away, whole body in frame

step_up.name: Step-Up
step_up.instruction: Stand facing a low step holding a rail. Step up with one foot, straighten that leg fully, bring the other foot up, then step down slowly. Alternate the leading leg. Safety: use a step no higher than 15 cm.
step_up.camera: side view, whole body and the step in frame

march_in_place.name: March in Place
march_in_place.instruction: Stand tall and march on the spot, lifting the knees to hip height if comfortable and swinging the arms, at a steady pace.
march_in_place.camera: side view, whole body in frame

condition_notes.HYPERTENSION: Because you have high blood pressure: breathe out as you lift and never hold your breath, and stop if you get a headache, blurred vision or feel dizzy.
condition_notes.DIABETES: Because you have diabetes: keep a sugary drink or snack nearby and stop if you feel shaky, sweaty or confused, which can mean low blood sugar. Wear well-fitting shoes and check your feet afterwards.
condition_notes.HEART_DISEASE: Because you have heart disease: warm up first, keep to the intensity in your plan, and stop straight away if you feel chest discomfort, unusual breathlessness or a racing heartbeat.
condition_notes.STROKE: Because you have had a stroke: exercise next to a sturdy support, go slowly on your weaker side, and stop if you notice new weakness, numbness or difficulty speaking.
condition_notes.ARTHRITIS: Because you have arthritis: some joint stiffness at the start is normal; move within a comfortable range and do not push into sharp joint pain.
condition_notes.OSTEOPOROSIS: Because you have osteoporosis: avoid twisting or bending forward sharply, and keep a support within reach to prevent falls.
condition_notes.ASTHMA: Because you have asthma: keep your reliever inhaler nearby and stop if you start wheezing or your chest feels tight.

limitation_notes.BALANCE_IMPAIRMENT: Because you declared a balance limitation: always keep one hand on a sturdy support.
limitation_notes.LEFT_LEG_MOBILITY: Go gently with your left leg and keep a support within reach.
limitation_notes.RIGHT_LEG_MOBILITY: Go gently with your right leg and keep a support within reach.
limitation_notes.LEFT_ARM_MOBILITY: Only move your left arm within a range that feels comfortable.
limitation_notes.RIGHT_ARM_MOBILITY: Only move your right arm within a range that feels comfortable.

risk_notes.High: Your risk level is High: follow your plan exactly as set and check with a healthcare professional before doing more.

late_night_note: It is {time} where you are. Late at night is not a good time for your exercises: tiredness and dim light raise the risk of a fall, and activity close to bedtime can disturb your sleep. Rest now and do them tomorrow, ideally in the late morning or late afternoon.

DIABETES.evening: With diabetes, avoid exercising late in the evening: it can make your blood sugar drop overnight. Exercise earlier in the day, about 1 to 3 hours after a meal.
DIABETES.late_night: With diabetes, exercising at night can make your blood sugar drop while you sleep.
DIABETES.early_morning: With diabetes, avoid exercising on an empty stomach first thing; have breakfast and exercise about 1 to 3 hours after it.
DIABETES.daytime: With diabetes, exercise about 1 to 3 hours after a meal rather than on an empty stomach.

HYPERTENSION.early_morning: Blood pressure is naturally higher in the first hours after waking: wait about an hour after you get up, warm up slowly and keep the effort gentle.

HEART_DISEASE.early_morning: Heart strain is more likely in the early morning: wait about an hour after waking, warm up slowly and avoid exercising right after a large meal.

ARTHRITIS.early_morning: Joints are often stiffest first thing in the morning: a warm shower and a few gentle movements first, or exercising later in the morning, can make it easier.

ASTHMA.early_morning: Cool morning air can trigger asthma: exercise indoors and warm up gradually.
ASTHMA.late_night: Cool night air can trigger asthma, another reason to wait until tomorrow.

OSTEOPOROSIS.early_morning: Make sure the room is well lit and the floor is clear: falls are more likely when you have just woken up.
OSTEOPOROSIS.evening: Make sure the room is well lit and the floor is clear: falls are more likely when it is dark or you are tired.

STROKE.evening: Exercise when you are not tired, with good lighting and someone nearby if possible.

BALANCE_IMPAIRMENT.early_morning: With your balance limitation, wait until you are fully awake and steady, and keep the room well lit.
BALANCE_IMPAIRMENT.evening: With your balance limitation, exercise in a well-lit room with someone nearby if possible.

now_notes.early_morning: It is {time} where you are. Early morning is fine once you have been up for a while, had something light to eat and warmed up.
now_notes.daytime: It is {time} where you are, a good time for your exercises if you feel well and have not just eaten a large meal.
now_notes.evening: It is {time} where you are. A session now is fine; finish at least an hour or two before bed so it does not disturb your sleep.

condition_detail.HYPERTENSION: With high blood pressure, regular gentle exercise like your plan can help lower it over time. Breathe out as you lift and never hold your breath or strain. If a home reading is 180/110 or higher, do not exercise that day: rest and contact your doctor.
condition_detail.DIABETES: With diabetes, exercise helps control your blood sugar. If you take insulin or tablets that can cause low sugar, check your level before you start and have a small snack if it is low; keep glucose sweets nearby, and stop if you feel shaky, sweaty or confused. Check your feet afterwards.
condition_detail.HEART_DISEASE: With heart disease, keep to the intensity in your plan: you should still be able to talk while exercising. Warm up and cool down for about five minutes. Stop at once if you get chest discomfort, unusual breathlessness, dizziness or a racing heartbeat, and call 999 if it does not settle with rest.
condition_detail.STROKE: After a stroke, these exercises help you regain strength and balance. Do them next to a sturdy support, go slowly on your weaker side, and stop and call 999 if you notice new weakness, numbness, a drooping face or slurred speech.
condition_detail.ARTHRITIS: With arthritis, moving keeps your joints flexible and the muscles around them strong. Some discomfort is fine if it settles within about two hours; if it lasts longer, do fewer repetitions next time. Rest a joint that is hot and swollen during a flare.
condition_detail.OSTEOPOROSIS: With osteoporosis, strengthening and standing exercises help your bones. Avoid bending forward from the waist, twisting and jerky movements, and keep a support within reach to prevent falls.
condition_detail.ASTHMA: With asthma, warm up gradually and keep your reliever inhaler within reach; use it before exercising if your doctor has told you to. Stop if you start wheezing or your chest feels tight, and avoid exercising in cold air or when your asthma is not well controlled.
condition_detail.PREGNANCY: During pregnancy, gentle exercise is usually safe and helpful when the pregnancy is going well, but check with your doctor or midwife first. After the first three months avoid lying flat on your back for long (as in the glute bridge), keep a support nearby for balance, drink water and do not overheat. Stop and contact your doctor if you have bleeding, dizziness, chest pain, calf pain or swelling, contractions or leaking fluid.
condition_detail.JOINT_REPLACEMENT: After a hip or knee replacement, your surgeon's and physiotherapist's exercises and precautions come first: they decide how far you may bend and when you may do more. After a new hip, avoid bending it past a right angle, crossing your legs and twisting until they say it is safe. Ask them before starting this plan, and stop if the wound becomes red, hot, swollen or more painful, or you get calf pain or a fever.

condition_closing: Your plan was chosen within the safety limits set from your health profile, so follow it as set and check with your doctor before doing more.

diet_notes.HYPERTENSION: With high blood pressure, keep salt low: your daily sodium limit is on the Home page.
diet_notes.DIABETES: With diabetes, spread carbohydrates through the day and exercise 1 to 3 hours after a meal; your daily sugar limit is on the Home page.
diet_notes.HEART_DISEASE: With heart disease, keep salt and saturated fat low and avoid exercising after a large meal.

red_flag_answer: Stop exercising now. If you have chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, sudden weakness or numbness, slurred speech, or severe swelling, call 999 or go to the nearest emergency department. For other new pain, dizziness or a fall, sit down, rest, and contact your doctor before exercising again.
